{{Short description|Measure of divisibility by a prime number}}
{{DISPLAYTITLE:{{mvar|p}}-adic valuation}}
In [[number theory]], the '''{{nowrap|{{mvar|p}}-adic}} valuation''' or '''{{mvar|p}}-adic order''' of an [[integer]] {{mvar|n}} is the [[exponent]] of the highest power of the [[prime number]] {{mvar|p}} that [[divides]] {{mvar|n}}.
It is denoted <math>\nu_p(n)</math>.
Equivalently, <math>\nu_p(n)</math> is the exponent to which <math>p</math> appears in the prime factorization of <math>n</math>.

The [[P-adic number|{{mvar|p}}-]]adic valuation is a [[Valuation (algebra)|valuation]] and gives rise to an analogue of the usual [[absolute value]], though unlike the latter, the {{mvar|p}}-adic absolute value is not [[Archimedean property|Archimedean]].
Whereas the [[Complete metric space|completion]] of the rational numbers with respect to the usual absolute value results in the [[real number]]s  <math>\mathbb{R}</math>, the completion of the rational numbers with respect to the {{mvar|p}}-adic absolute value results in the [[p-adic number|{{nowrap|{{mvar|p}}-adic}} numbers]] <math>\mathbb{Q}_p</math>.<ref>
{{cite book
 | first1= David S.|last1= Dummit
 |first2=Richard M. |last2=Foote
 | year = 2003
 | title = Abstract Algebra
 | edition = 3rd
 | publisher = Wiley
 | isbn = 0-471-43334-9
 | pages = 758–759
}}</ref>
[[Image:2adic12480.svg|thumb|right|200px|Distribution of natural numbers by their 2-adic valuation, labeled with corresponding [[power of two|powers of two]] in decimal. Zero has an infinite valuation.]]

==Definition and properties==
Let {{mvar|p}} be a [[prime number]].

===Integers===
The '''{{mvar|p}}-adic valuation''' of an integer <math>n</math> is defined to be
:<math>
\nu_p(n)=
\begin{cases}
\mathrm{max}\{k \in \mathbb{N}_0 : p^k \mid n\} & \text{if } n \neq 0\\
\infty & \text{if } n=0,
\end{cases}
</math>
where <math>\mathbb{N}_0</math> denotes the set of [[natural number]]s (including zero) and <math>m \mid n</math> denotes [[divisor|divisibility]] of <math>n</math> by <math>m</math>. In particular, <math>\nu_p</math> is a function <math>\nu_p \colon \mathbb{Z} \to \mathbb{N}_0 \cup\{\infty\} </math>.<ref>{{cite book|last1=Ireland |first1=K. |last2=Rosen |first2=M. |date=2000 |title=A Classical Introduction to Modern Number Theory |publisher=Springer-Verlag |location=New York |page=3}}{{ISBN needed}}</ref>

For example, <math>\nu_2(-12) = 2</math>, <math>\nu_3(-12) = 1</math>, and <math>\nu_5(-12) = 0</math> since <math>|{-12}| = 12 = 2^2 \cdot 3^1 \cdot 5^0</math>.

The notation <math>p^k \parallel n</math> is sometimes used to mean <math>k = \nu_p(n)</math>.<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Niven |first1=Ivan |author1-link=Ivan M. Niven |last2=Zuckerman |first2=Herbert S. |last3=Montgomery |first3=Hugh L. |author3-link=Hugh Lowell Montgomery |title=An Introduction to the Theory of Numbers |date=1991 |publisher=[[John Wiley & Sons]] |edition=5th |isbn=0-471-62546-9 |page=4}}</ref>

If <math>n</math> is a positive integer, then <math>\nu_p(n) \leq \log_p n</math>; this follows directly from <math>n \geq p^{\nu_p(n)}</math>.

===Rational numbers===
The {{mvar|p}}-adic valuation can be extended to the [[rational number]]s as the function

:<math>\nu_p : \mathbb{Q} \to \mathbb{Z} \cup\{\infty\} </math><ref name="infty">with the usual order relation, namely
:<math>\infty > n</math>,
and rules for arithmetic operations,
:<math>\infty + n = n + \infty = \infty</math>,
on the extended number line.</ref><ref>{{cite book|last1=Khrennikov |first1=A. |last2=Nilsson |first2=M. |date=2004 |title={{mvar|p}}-adic Deterministic and Random Dynamics |publisher=Kluwer Academic Publishers |page=9}}{{ISBN needed}}</ref>

defined by

:<math>
\nu_p\left(\frac{r}{s}\right)=\nu_p(r)-\nu_p(s).
</math>

For example, <math>\nu_2 \bigl(\tfrac{9}{8}\bigr) = -3</math> and <math>\nu_3 \bigl(\tfrac{9}{8}\bigr) = 2</math> since <math>\tfrac{9}{8} = 2^{-3}\cdot 3^2</math>.

Some properties are:
 
:<math>\nu_p(r\cdot s) = \nu_p(r) + \nu_p(s)</math>
:<math>\nu_p(r+s) \geq \min\bigl\{ \nu_p(r), \nu_p(s)\bigr\}</math>

Moreover, if <math>\nu_p(r) \neq \nu_p(s)</math>, then

:<math>\nu_p(r+s)= \min\bigl\{ \nu_p(r), \nu_p(s)\bigr\}</math>

where <math>\min</math> is the minimum (i.e. the smaller of the two).

=== Formula for the {{mvar|p}}-adic valuation of integers ===
[[Legendre's formula]] shows that <math>\nu_p(n!)=\sum_{i=1}^{\infty{}}{\left\lfloor{\frac{n}{p^i}}\right\rfloor{}}</math>. 

For any positive integer {{mvar|n}}, <math>n = \frac{n!}{(n-1)!}</math> and so <math>\nu_p(n)=\nu_p(n!)-\nu_p((n-1)!)</math>.

Therefore, <math>\nu{}_p(n)=\sum_{i=1}^{\infty{}}{\bigg(\left\lfloor{\frac{n}{p^i}}\right\rfloor{}-\left\lfloor{\frac{n-1}{p^i}}\right\rfloor{}\bigg)}</math>.

This infinite sum can be reduced to <math>\sum_{i=1}^{\lfloor{\log_p{(n)}\rfloor{}}}{\bigg(\left\lfloor{\frac{n}{p^i}}\right\rfloor{}-\left\lfloor{\frac{n-1}{p^i}}\right\rfloor{}\bigg)}</math>.

This formula can be extended to negative integer values to give:

<math>\nu{}_p(n) =\sum_{i=1}^{\lfloor{\log_p{(|n|)}\rfloor{}}}{\bigg(\left\lfloor{\frac{|n|}{p^i}}\right\rfloor{}-\left\lfloor{\frac{|n|-1}{p^i}}\right\rfloor{}\bigg)}</math>

=={{mvar|p}}-adic absolute value==
{{anchor|p-adic norm}}

The {{mvar|p}}-adic [[Absolute value (algebra)|absolute value]] (or {{mvar|p}}-adic norm,<ref>{{cite book
 | last = Murty | first = M. Ram
 | doi = 10.1007/978-1-4757-3441-6
 | isbn = 0-387-95143-1
 | mr = 1803093
 | pages = 147–148
 | publisher = Springer-Verlag, New York
 | series = Graduate Texts in Mathematics
 | title = Problems in analytic number theory
 | volume = 206
 | year = 2001}}</ref> though not a [[norm (mathematics)|norm]] in the sense of analysis) on [[rational number|<math>\mathbb{Q}</math>]] is the function 
:<math>|\cdot|_p \colon \Q \to \R_{\ge 0} </math>
defined by
:<math>|r|_p = p^{-\nu_p(r)} .</math>

Thereby, <math>|0|_p = p^{-\infty} = 0</math> for all <math>p</math> and 
for example, <math>|{-12}|_2 = 2^{-2} = \tfrac{1}{4}</math> and <math>\bigl|\tfrac{9}{8}\bigr|_2 = 2^{-(-3)} = 8 .</math>

The {{mvar|p}}-adic absolute value satisfies the following properties.

:{| class="wikitable"
|-
|Non-negativity || <math>|r|_p \geq 0</math>
|-
|[[Positive-definite function|Positive-definiteness]] || <math>|r|_p = 0 \iff r = 0</math>
|-
|[[Multiplicative function|Multiplicativity]] || <math>|r s|_p = |r|_p|s|_p</math>
|-
|[[Ultrametric space|Non-Archimedean]] || <math>|r+s|_p \leq \max\left(|r|_p, |s|_p\right)</math>
|}
From the [[Multiplicative function|multiplicativity]] <math>|r s|_p = |r|_p|s|_p</math> it follows that <math>|1|_p=1=|{-1}|_p</math> for the [[root of unity|roots of unity]] <math>1</math> and <math>-1</math> and consequently also <math>|{-r}|_p = |r|_p .</math>
The [[subadditivity]] <math>|r+s|_p \leq |r|_p + |s|_p</math> follows from the [[Ultrametric space|non-Archimedean]] [[triangle inequality]] <math>|r+s|_p \leq \max\left(|r|_p, |s|_p\right)</math>.

===Product formula===
The choice of base {{mvar|p}} in the [[exponentiation]] <math>p^{-\nu_p(r)} </math> makes no difference for most of the properties, but supports the product formula:
:<math>\prod_{0, p} |r|_p = 1</math>
where the product is taken over all primes {{mvar|p}} and the usual absolute value, denoted <math>|r|_0</math>. This follows from simply taking the [[prime factorization]]: each prime power factor <math>p^k</math> contributes its reciprocal to its {{mvar|p}}-adic absolute value, and then the usual [[Archimedean property|Archimedean]] absolute value cancels all of them.

By [[Ostrowski's theorem]], the usual and {{mvar|p}}-adic absolute values occurring in the formula are all the absolute values on the rational numbers up to equivalence. An analogous product formula can be used to axiomatically define [[global field]]s, of which the rational numbers are the simplest example.

===Metric and completion===
A [[metric space]] can be formed on the set <math>\mathbb{Q}</math> with a ([[Ultrametric space|non-Archimedean]], [[Translation invariance|translation-invariant]]) metric
:<math>d \colon \Q \times \Q \to \R_{\ge 0} </math>
defined by
:<math>d(r,s) = |r-s|_p .</math>
The [[Complete metric space|completion]] of <math>\mathbb{Q}</math> with respect to this metric leads to the set <math>\mathbb{Q}_p</math> of {{mvar|p}}-adic numbers. Like the rationals, they form a [[field (mathematics)|field]], and the {{mvar|p}}-adic valuation and absolute value can be extended to <math>\mathbb{Q}_p</math>, making it a [[complete valued field]].
